section_summary: This section closes an earlier letter from Joseph C. Grew on Japan’s administrative control of immigration and alien landholding, followed by translations of 1899 ordinances restricting alien laborers. Most of the section concerns Japan’s 1939 immigration ordinance, including diplomatic reports, an internal State Department discussion rejecting “retaliation in kind,” and a full English translation of the new rules on entry, registration, residence, travel, fees, policing, and deportation. The final pages are cross-reference sheets directing researchers to related despatches and a Japanese Embassy note.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of Grew letter on administrative control of immigration and alien landholding
subfiles.about: Grew concludes that Japanese immigration and alien landholding controls depend principally on administrative action rather than statute.
subfiles.summary: Grew's concluding page: administrative action is the center of Japan's immigration controls and partly of landownership limits; officials are unlikely to be criticized for extra-legal measures; ordinance translation enclosed.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 352 concerning alien residence and employment
subfiles.from: Emperor of Japan, with the approval of the Privy Council
subfiles.about: The ordinance regulates residence and employment by aliens lacking treaty-based freedom of residence.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Ordinance 352 lets covered aliens live and trade outside the former settlements, excluding laborers without special permission; fines up to one hundred yen; effective August 4, 1899.

subfiles.title: Home Department Ordinance No. 421 implementing Imperial Ordinance No. 352
subfiles.to: Prefectural governors and the governor of Hokkaido
subfiles.about: The ordinance identifies the officials and occupations covered by the 1899 restrictions on alien labor.
subfiles.summary: Home Department Ordinance 421 gives prefectural governors authority, defines alien laborers across agriculture, fishing, mining, construction and other work, excludes domestic servants, and lets governors revoke permits for public welfare.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 421: New Japanese Immigration Regulations Announced
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch reports newspaper accounts of forthcoming Japanese immigration regulations scheduled for enforcement in May 1939.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 421: new immigration rules replacing the 1918 regulations would require more police registration, heavier penalties, summary expulsion of suspected immoral persons, communists or spies, and entry and transit fees.

subfiles.title: Note suggesting consideration of retaliation in kind
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks whether the United States should consider retaliatory action against Japanese immigration restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck suggests considering action characterized as retaliation in kind for a marked passage in the attachment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed retaliation for Japanese controls over foreigners
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs; drafted by Salisbury
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates and rejects retaliation against Japanese nationals in response to Japan’s new controls over foreign residents and tourists.
subfiles.summary: Memo recommends against retaliating for Home Office Ordinance 6, requiring foreign residents' police certificates and tourist registration, as impractical, unfair given Soviet and European measures, and unimportant enough to compromise principles; summarizes Report 49.

subfiles.title: Report No. 49: Promulgation of New Japanese Immigration Regulations
subfiles.from: Thomas Q. Hickok, American Consul; approved by C. R. Cameron
subfiles.about: The report explains the newly promulgated Japanese ordinance governing foreign entry, residence, registration, travel, and departure.
subfiles.summary: Hickok reports that Home Office Ordinance No. 6 was promulgated on March 1, 1939, and would become effective on May 1. Approximately forty thousand foreign residents would have to apply annually for permission to remain and separately notify their local police, while hotels and other lodging providers would report detailed information about foreign guests. The ordinance establishes entry and passage visas, special-permission fees, travel certificates for China and Manchukuo, departure notification, deportation categories, and penalties of fines or up to three months’ imprisonment. It repeals the immigration ordinance dating from 1918.

subfiles.title: Concerning Entry into, Sojourn in and Departure from Japan of Foreigners
subfiles.from: Japanese Home and Foreign Ministers; English translation published by the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.to: Foreigners entering, residing in, or departing from Japan
subfiles.about: The twenty-article ordinance establishes detailed rules for the admission, registration, residence, travel, policing, and deportation of foreigners.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance distinguishes entry stays of fifteen days or more from shorter passage visits and lists six categories of persons subject to exclusion. It requires inspection at ports of entry, applications for longer stays, police notification by foreign residents, reporting by lodging providers, and truthful responses to police inquiries. Additional provisions create residence and travel certificates, impose reciprocal or special-permission fees, require departure notification after longer stays, and authorize deportation for specified violations. The ordinance provides fines, detention, or imprisonment for noncompliance, takes effect May 1, 1939, and abolishes the January 1918 ordinance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 3825 on new Japanese alien regulations
subfiles.about: The file note redirects researchers to Despatch No. 3825 concerning Japan’s new rules for alien entry, sojourn, and departure.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grew's Despatch 3825 of April 12, 1939 on new Japanese alien regulations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Embassy Note No. 106
subfiles.about: The file note points to a Japanese Embassy submission containing translations of regulations on alien residence, trade, travel, entry, sojourn, and departure.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japanese Embassy Note 106 with a translation of Home Department Ordinance 6 and a revision of the entry ordinance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 3868 transmitting an ordinance translation
subfiles.about: The file note redirects researchers to a Grew despatch transmitting a translation of Japan’s ordinance on alien entry, sojourn, and departure.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Despatch 3868 of May 6, 1939 transmitting the ordinance translation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 3969 transmitting a revised ordinance
subfiles.about: The file note redirects researchers to a Dooman despatch transmitting a translation of a revision to Japan’s alien entry, sojourn, and departure ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Dooman's Despatch 3969 of June 19, 1939 on a translated revision of the alien ordinance.
